claims.text: Active-learning interatomic potentials can accurately reproduce the free energies of both solid and fluid phases near fusion.
The proposed potentials can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
Elemental and binary metallic systems have previously been benchmarked for the proposed type of calculation.
The method can be extended from elemental and binary metals to multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The proposed framework will iteratively train interatomic potentials on ab initio reference configurations generated using enhanced sampling such as metadynamics or parallel tempering.
Enhanced sampling will target configurational regions needed to capture anharmonic and entropy contributions in both solid and fluid phases.
The method is intended for temperatures near melting and for systems ranging from elemental and binary metals to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced sampling effectively explores the relevant parts of the potential-energy surface.
The active-learning loop captures average and rare-event configurations important for free-energy evaluation.
Replacing full ab initio molecular dynamics with a potential trained on representative configurations maintains free-energy fidelity while reducing computational expense.
Systematic active-learning refinement ensures transferability and captures subtle anharmonic effects.
The computational cost will be reduced by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Free-energy predictions and phase-transition temperatures will have accuracy comparable to TOR-TILD for elemental and binary systems.
Comparable free-energy fidelity is expected to persist in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Vibrational and configurational entropy can contribute to the thermodynamic stabilization of high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning models can predict static FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy properties with mean relative errors within 5% on the reported PtPd-based dataset.
Performance is expected to be reliable for metallic systems whose bonding environments resemble those in the training data.
Accuracy may be uncertain for systems with very strong electron–vibration coupling or extreme anharmonicity outside the tested regime.
A deviation greater than 10% in benchmark phase free energies or associated thermodynamic observables, or failure to capture key anharmonic effects, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that systematic refinement ensures transferability and retention of all entropy contributions, whereas the uncertainty field says transferability and robustness in capturing those contributions are not established for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.

The hypothesis broadly claims accurate retention of electron–vibration coupling and anharmonicity, while the boundary explicitly concedes uncertain accuracy for strong electron–vibration coupling or extreme anharmonicity. This can be reconciled only by restricting the hypothesis to the stated boundary.
